relationship: related regnal references to an earthquake
rationale: Amos dates its words two years before an earthquake during Uzziah's reign in Judah. Zechariah compares a blocked ravine with its blocking in the earthquake in the days of Oziah king of Judah. The earthquake and royal dating supply the comparison; the given name forms and the different uses of the event are preserved.
source_text: The words of Amos that came among nakkarim from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.

target_units.text: The ravine of My mountains will be blocked; the mountain ravine will be joined as far as Iasol and blocked as it was blocked in the days of the earthquake, in the days of Oziah king of Judah. The Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him.

relationship: close pairing of the Lord's voice from Zion and Jerusalem
rationale: Both passages pair the Lord's voice from Zion with His voice from Jerusalem. Amos describes mourning pastures and a dried Carmel summit, while Joel describes shaking heaven and earth and the Lord sparing and strengthening His people. The opening declaration closely corresponds despite the different consequences.
source_text: He said: “The Lord spoke from Zion and gave His voice from Jerusalem; the shepherds’ pastures mourned, and Carmel’s summit dried up.”

target_units.text: The Lord will cry out from Zion and give His voice from Jerusalem; heaven and earth will shake. But the Lord will spare His people, and the Lord will strengthen the sons of Israel.

relationship: related Syrian violence against pregnant women
rationale: Amos condemns Damascus for sawing pregnant women in Gilead with iron saws. Elisha tells Hazael of the evil he will do to Israel, including tearing open pregnant women; the surrounding account names his future Syrian kingship. The particular atrocity connects them, while method, location and reported versus predicted action differ.
source_text: The Lord said: “For three impieties of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they sawed the pregnant women of those in Gilead with iron saws.

target_units.text: Hazael said, ‘Why does my lord weep?’ He said, ‘Because I know all the evils you will do to the sons of Israel: you will send their strongholds into fire, kill their chosen men with the sword, dash down their infants, and tear open their pregnant women.’

relationship: parallel fire consuming buildings associated with Ader's son
rationale: Amos threatens fire in Hazael's house that consumes the foundations of the son of Ader. Jeremiah threatens fire in Damascus's wall that consumes the quarters of Ader's son. The named designation and consuming fire are shared; foundations and quarters remain the supplied building descriptions.
source_text: I will send fire into Hazael’s house, and it will devour the foundations of the son of Ader,

target_units.text: I will kindle fire in Damascus’s wall, and it will devour the quarters of Ader’s son.

relationship: parallel judgment removing Damascus's strength and affecting Syria
rationale: Amos announces shattered Damascus bars and the captivity of Syria's people, alongside other named removals. Isaiah announces ruined Damascus, the loss of its kingdom and the perishing of the Syrians' remainder. Both connect Damascus's collapse with Syria's fate, while captivity and perishing are different outcomes.
source_text: and I will shatter Damascus’s bars and destroy inhabitants from the Plain of On. I will cut down a tribe from the men of Harran, and the people of Syria, called by name, will be taken captive,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: The utterance against Damascus. Behold, Damascus will be removed from the cities and become a ruin,
abandoned for everlasting time, a bed and resting place for flocks, with no one pursuing.

There will no longer be a stronghold for Ephraim to flee to, nor a kingdom in Damascus, and the Syrians’ remainder will perish; for you are no better than Israel’s sons and their glory. Thus says the Lord Sabaoth.

relationship: same-chapter paired accusations concerning Solomon's captives and Idumea
rationale: The Gaza accusation describes taking Solomon's captives into captivity to shut them up in Idumea. The Tyre accusation likewise names Solomon's captives shut up in Idumea, adding the forgotten covenant of brothers. The unusual captive designation and destination connect the charges without asserting one shared incident.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they took Solomon’s captives into captivity, to shut them up in Idumea.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn away from her, because they shut Solomon’s captives up in Idumea and did not remember a covenant of brothers.

relationship: same-chapter repeated fire judgment upon walls and foundations
rationale: The sentence against Gaza and the sentence against Tyre both announce God sending fire upon the city's walls and consuming its foundations. The repeated complete judgment formula gives the two separate city oracles a particular structural correspondence.
source_text: I will send fire upon Gaza’s walls, and it will devour her foundations.

target_units.text: I will send fire upon Tyre’s walls, and it will devour her foundations.”

relationship: different announced outcomes involving Azotus and foreigners
rationale: Amos announces destruction of Azotus's inhabitants and the perishing of the remaining foreigners. Zechariah announces foreigners dwelling in Azotus and the bringing down of their arrogance. The city and foreigners language connect the oracles, while dwelling and destruction are not treated as the same outcome.
source_text: I will destroy inhabitants from Azotus, and a tribe will be removed from Ascalon. I will bring My hand against Accaron, and the remaining foreigners will perish,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: Foreigners will dwell in Azotus, and I will bring down the foreigners’ arrogance.

relationship: related accusations against Tyre concerning captives
rationale: Amos condemns Tyre for confining Solomon's captives in Idumea and forgetting a covenant of brothers. Joel's address to Tyre and the other named regions condemns selling Judah and Jerusalem's sons to the Greeks. Both accuse Tyre concerning captives; confinement, sale and the supplied destinations remain distinct.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn away from her, because they shut Solomon’s captives up in Idumea and did not remember a covenant of brothers.

target_units.text: and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, so as to thrust them out of their own borders.

relationship: parallel fire judgment upon fortified Tyre
rationale: Amos threatens fire on Tyre's walls that will consume her foundations. Zechariah describes Tyre building fortifications and announces that she will be consumed by fire. The named fortified city and fiery judgment connect the oracles, while Zechariah also describes her wealth and strength struck into the sea.
source_text: I will send fire upon Tyre’s walls, and it will devour her foundations.”

target_units.text: Tyre built herself fortifications, stored silver like dust and gathered gold like the mud of the roads.
Therefore the Lord will inherit her and strike her strength into the sea; she will be consumed by fire.

relationship: parallel condemnation of Idumea for violence toward a brother
rationale: Amos condemns Idumea for pursuing a brother with a sword, amid its other violent acts. Obadiah condemns slaughter and impiety toward brother Jacob within its address to Idumea. Violence against a brother is shared, while Obadiah explicitly names Jacob.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Idumea, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they pursued his brother with a sword; he ravaged a womb upon the earth, seized his shuddering as testimony, and kept his onrush for victory.

target_units.text: because of the slaughter and the impiety toward your brother Jacob; and shame will cover you, and you will be removed forever.

relationship: parallel divine judgment upon Teman's habitations
rationale: Amos threatens fire consuming Teman's wall foundations. Jeremiah names the Lord's purpose against Teman's inhabitants and says their dwelling will be made untrodden. Teman and the ruin of its inhabited structures connect the judgments; fire is explicit in Amos.
source_text: I will send fire into Teman, and it will devour the foundations of her walls.”

target_units.text: Therefore hear the Lord’s counsel that He planned against Idumea and His purpose against Teman’s inhabitants: Surely the smallest sheep will be swept together; surely their dwelling will be made untrodden over her.

relationship: parallel atrocity of ripping open pregnant women
rationale: Amos condemns Ammon's sons for ripping open Gileadite pregnant women to enlarge their borders. Kings reports Manaem striking Thersa and ripping open pregnant women because the place did not open to him. The particular violent act is shared, with different perpetrators, places and stated motives.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they ripped open the pregnant women of the Gileadites in order to enlarge their borders.

target_units.text: Then Manaem struck Thersa, everything in it, and its territory from Thersa, because they did not open to him. He struck it and ripped open the pregnant women.

relationship: parallel fire and the din of war in the Ammon oracles
rationale: Amos joins fire against Rabbah's walls and foundations with shouting on the day of war. Jeremiah's Ammon oracle joins the din of wars against Rabbath with burned altars and destruction. War noise and fire connect them; the supplied place forms and burned structures remain distinct.
source_text: I will kindle fire upon Rabbah’s walls, and it will devour her foundations with shouting on the day of war; she will be shaken on the day of her end.

target_units.text: Therefore days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make the din of wars heard against Rabbath. They will become an untrodden place and a destruction, her altars will be burned with fire, and Israel will receive his rule.

relationship: close collective deportation of priests and rulers with a leading figure
rationale: Amos says her kings will go into captivity with their priests and rulers. Jeremiah says Melchom will go into deportation with his priests and rulers. The collective priest-and-ruler deportation closely corresponds, while Amos's plural kings are not silently identified with the target's named Melchom.
source_text: Her kings will go into captivity, their priests and their rulers together,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: Shout aloud, Heshbon, for Gai perished! Cry out, daughters of Rabbath; put on sackcloth, be seized with distress, and beat yourselves over Melchom, for he will go into deportation, his priests and rulers together.

relationship: contrast in the burning of human bones
rationale: Amos condemns Moab for burning the bones of Idumea's king into lime. Kings describes Josiah burning bones from tombs upon Bethel's altar to defile it, according to the Lord's word, while sparing other bones. The physical action is related, but its purpose and assessment differ sharply between the passages.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they burned the bones of Idumea’s king into lime.

target_units.text: Josiah turned aside and saw the tombs there in the city. He sent and took the bones from the tombs, burned them on the altar, and defiled it, according to the Lord’s word which the man of God spoke while Jeroboam stood at the festival beside the altar. Turning, he lifted his eyes toward the tomb of the man of God who had spoken these words.
He said, ‘What is that rocky marker I see?’ The city’s men told him, ‘It is the man of God who came out of Judah and proclaimed these words which he proclaimed against Bethel’s altar.’
He said, ‘Leave it alone. Let no one move his bones.’ His bones were spared together with the bones of the prophet who came from Samaria.

relationship: repeated pairing of fire and war shouting in distinct national oracles
rationale: The Moab judgment combines fire consuming city foundations with weakness, shouting and trumpet sound. The Rabbah judgment combines fire consuming foundations with shouting on the day of war. Their repeated fire-and-shouting combination connects the separate national judgments, while the trumpet is particular to Moab's unit.
source_text: I will send fire upon Moab, and it will devour the foundations of her cities. Moab will die in weakness, with shouting and the sound of a trumpet.

target_units.text: I will kindle fire upon Rabbah’s walls, and it will devour her foundations with shouting on the day of war; she will be shaken on the day of her end.

relationship: parallel rejection of divine commands and pursuit of vain things
rationale: Amos accuses Judah of rejecting the Lord's law, failing to keep His ordinances and being led astray by vain things. Kings describes Israel failing to keep His testimonies, following vain things and abandoning His commandments. The two-part indictment closely corresponds across the differently identified peoples.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of the sons of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they rejected the Lord’s law and did not keep His ordinances. Their vain things, which they made, led them astray—the things their fathers followed.

target_units.text: They did not keep His testimonies by which He warned them. They followed vain things and became vain, and followed the nations around them, concerning whom He had commanded them not to do such things.
They abandoned the commandments of the Lord their God. They made a casting for themselves, two heifers, made groves, bowed down to all heaven’s host, and served Baal.

relationship: parallel divine fire consuming Jerusalem's buildings
rationale: Amos announces fire in Judah consuming Jerusalem's foundations. Jeremiah conditionally warns of fire in Jerusalem's gates consuming her quarters if the people do not consecrate the Sabbath. The Lord's fire upon the same city's structures connects them; Jeremiah supplies the particular Sabbath condition.
source_text: I will send fire upon Judah, and it will devour Jerusalem’s foundations.”

target_units.text: And if you do not listen to Me to consecrate the Sabbath day, not lifting burdens and not entering Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath day, I will kindle fire in her gates, and it will devour Jerusalem’s quarters and not be extinguished.

relationship: repeated trading of vulnerable people for silver and sandals
rationale: The earlier accusation names the righteous sold for silver and the poor for sandals. The later commercial speech names acquiring the poor for silver and the lowly for sandals. The repeated forms of payment make the connection particular, while selling and acquiring describe different sides of exploitation.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they sold a righteous person for silver and a poor person for sandals,

target_units.text: to acquire the poor with silver and a lowly person in exchange for sandals? And we will trade from every kind of produce.”

relationship: related oppression expressed through turning aside the lowly
rationale: Amos describes fists upon poor people's heads and turning aside the way of the humble. Isaiah condemns turning aside the poor's judgment and seizing the needy people's justice. Oppression and the turning-aside language connect them; Isaiah explicitly focuses on legal judgment.
source_text: which tread upon the earth’s dust. They struck the heads of the poor with their fists and turned aside the way of the humble; a son and his father went in to the same young slave woman, to profane the name of their God,

target_units.text: turning aside the judgment of the poor, seizing the justice of My people’s needy, so that a widow becomes their prey and an orphan their plunder.

relationship: related use of oppressively acquired goods in a sacred setting
rationale: Amos places drinking wine from extortions in the house of their God. Malachi criticizes bringing things seized by force among the sacrifices. Both associate goods gained through wrongdoing with a sacred setting; Amos describes drinking and does not explicitly call the wine a sacrifice.
source_text: and, tying their garments with cords, they made hangings next to the altar, and drank wine from extortions in their God’s house.

target_units.text: “And you said, ‘These things are from hardship,’ and I blew them away,” says the Lord Almighty. “You were bringing things seized by force, the lame and the afflicted. If you bring the sacrifice, shall I accept these things from your hands?” says the Lord Almighty.

relationship: parallel ruin of roots below and produce above
rationale: Amos describes removing the Amorite's fruit above and roots below. In Bildad's speech, roots dry up below and the harvest falls above. The paired vertical image expresses comprehensive ruin, with national judgment in Amos and the account of the unjust in Job's surrounding speech.
source_text: But I removed the Amorite from before them, whose height was like a cedar and who was strong as an oak. I removed his fruit above and his roots below.

target_units.text: Below, his roots will dry up; above, his harvest will fall.

relationship: shared recollection of divine guidance through forty wilderness years
rationale: Amos recalls God bringing Israel from Egypt and guiding them forty years in the wilderness to inherit the Amorite's land. Deuteronomy recalls the Lord's wilderness guidance, feeding and the forty years. The period and divine guidance connect them, with inheritance emphasized in Amos and testing and instruction in Deuteronomy.
source_text: I brought you up from Egypt’s land and led you around in the wilderness forty years, to inherit the Amorites’ land.

target_units.text: And you shall remember all the way wherein the Lord your God led you in the wilderness, to afflict you and to test you, that the things in your heart might be known, whether you would keep His commandments or not.

And He afflicted you, and made you hunger, and fed you with manna, which your fathers did not know, that He might declare unto you that man shall not live by bread alone, but man shall live by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God.
Your garments did not wear out upon you, neither did your feet become calloused; behold, these forty years.

relationship: divine appointment of prophets from within the people
rationale: Amos recalls God taking some of the people's sons as prophets, alongside young men for consecration. Deuteronomy promises a prophet raised by the Lord from among their brothers. Both place prophetic appointment with God and its human origin within the people, while taking and raising remain the respective verbs.
source_text: I took some of your sons as prophets and some of your young men for consecration. Are these things not so, sons of Israel?” says the Lord.

target_units.text: The Lord your God shall raise up unto you a prophet from among your brethren, like unto me; you shall hearken unto him,

relationship: contrast between consecration from wine and giving wine to the consecrated
rationale: Amos accuses the people of giving wine to those consecrated. Numbers describes a vow of consecration to the Lord involving separation from wine and strong drink. The wine given in Amos contrasts directly with the abstinence specified for consecration in the law.
source_text: “But you gave the consecrated ones wine to drink and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘You must not prophesy!’

target_units.text: Speak unto the sons of Israel, and you shall say unto them: If a man or woman solemnly vows a vow of consecration unto the Lord, to be set apart

from wine and strong drink, he shall be purified from wine. He shall drink neither vinegar of wine, nor vinegar of strong drink, nor anything prepared from grapes; and he shall eat neither fresh grapes nor raisins.

relationship: parallel commands silencing prophetic speech
rationale: Amos quotes a command to the prophets not to prophesy. Isaiah describes people telling prophets not to announce and visionaries not to speak, instead demanding another deception. The shared prohibition of prophetic speech connects the passages; Isaiah additionally states the desired substitute.
source_text: “But you gave the consecrated ones wine to drink and commanded the prophets, saying, ‘You must not prophesy!’

target_units.text: who say to the prophets, “Do not announce to us,” and to those seeing visions, “Do not speak to us. Instead, speak to us and announce another deception,

relationship: parallel failure of military strength to save
rationale: Amos says the strong will not retain strength and the fighter will not save his life, alongside failed flight. The psalm says a king is not saved by a great force and a giant is not saved by abundant strength. Both deny rescue through martial capacity, with different representative figures.
source_text: and flight will perish from the runner, the mighty one will certainly not maintain his strength, and the fighter will certainly not save his life,

target_units.text: A king is not saved through a great force, and a giant will not be saved by the abundance of his strength.

relationship: related failure of confidence associated with horses
rationale: Amos includes the horse rider among those who will not save their lives. The psalm calls a horse false for salvation and says its abundant power will not save it. The specific horse-and-salvation pairing connects the warnings, while Amos explicitly focuses on the rider.
source_text: and the archer will certainly not stand, the swift of foot will certainly not be saved, nor will the horseman save his life,

target_units.text: A horse is false for salvation, and by the abundance of its power it will not be saved.

relationship: judgment of the people associated with recollection of the exodus
rationale: Amos introduces the Lord's word against the tribes He brought from Egypt. Micah likewise announces the Lord's case against Israel and recalls bringing them from Egypt and the house of slavery. Both join the judgment address to that remembered deliverance.
source_text: Hear this word that the Lord spoke against you, house of Israel, and against every tribe I brought up from Egypt’s land, saying:

target_units.text: Hear, hills, the Lord’s judgment, and you ravines, foundations of the earth! For the Lord has a case against His people, and He will argue it with Israel.
“My people, what have I done to you? How have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer Me!
For I brought you up from Egypt’s land and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam before you.

relationship: election accompanied by accountability to God
rationale: Amos joins the Lord's unique knowledge of Israel among the earth's tribes with judgment for its sins. Deuteronomy likewise identifies Israel as God's chosen possession among the nations and describes both covenant mercy and repayment to those who hate Him. Their privileged relationship does not remove accountability.
source_text: “You alone have I known among all the earth’s tribes; therefore I will exact judgment upon you for all your sins.”

target_units.text: For you are a holy people unto the Lord your God; and the Lord your God has chosen you to be unto Him a people for His own possession, above all the nations upon the face of the earth.
The Lord preferred you and chose you, not because you were more numerous than all the nations, for you are the fewest of all the nations,

but because the Lord loved you, and kept the oath which He sware unto your fathers, the Lord brought you forth with a mighty hand and with an uplifted arm, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, out of the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
And you shall know that the Lord your God, He is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and mercy with them that love Him and keep His commandments, unto a thousand generations,
and repays them that hate Him to their face, to destroy them. He shall not delay with them that hate Him; He shall repay them to their face.

relationship: lion's voice associated with captured prey
rationale: Amos asks whether a lion roars without prey or a young lion voices itself without a seizure. Isaiah explicitly depicts a lion or cub crying over prey it has caught. The shared animal behavior grounds different prophetic comparisons in the two passages.
source_text: Will a lion roar from its thicket without prey? Will a young lion give its voice from its enclosure at all unless it has seized something?

target_units.text: For thus the Lord said to me: “As a lion or lion cub cries over prey it has caught and shouts over it until the mountains fill with its voice, and they are defeated and terrified by the greatness of its wrath, so the Lord Sabaoth will descend to march upon Mount Zion, upon her mountains.

relationship: bird-catching imagery associated with danger
rationale: Amos pairs the bird, fowler and sprung trap in questions about a catch. Ecclesiastes similarly uses birds caught in a snare to picture people overtaken by an evil time. Both draw their warning imagery from actual capture of a bird, while their immediate argumentative uses differ.
source_text: Will a bird fall upon the ground without a fowler? Will a trap be sprung upon the ground without catching something?

target_units.text: For a person does not know his time: like fish caught in an evil net, and birds caught in a snare, so human beings are trapped at an evil time when it falls upon them suddenly.

relationship: trumpet alarm affecting a city's inhabitants
rationale: Amos asks whether a trumpet can sound in a city without alarming its people. Joel commands a trumpet in Zion and turmoil among the land's inhabitants because the Lord's day is near. The warning sound and alarmed response connect the texts.
source_text: Will a trumpet sound in a city and the people not be alarmed? Will there be calamity in a city that the Lord has not done?

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Proclaim on My holy mountain, and let all who inhabit the land be thrown into turmoil, because the Lord’s day is present; it is near,

relationship: the Lord identified as the agent of calamity
rationale: Amos asks whether a city's calamity occurs without the Lord having done it. Isaiah identifies the Lord as making peace and creating calamities. Both explicitly connect calamity with His agency, while Isaiah also names His making of light and darkness.
source_text: Will a trumpet sound in a city and the people not be alarmed? Will there be calamity in a city that the Lord has not done?

target_units.text: I fashioned light and made darkness; I make peace and create calamities. I am the Lord God, who does all these things.

relationship: the Lord discloses His purpose to a servant
rationale: Amos says the Lord reveals His discipline to His servants the prophets before acting. Genesis records the Lord asking whether to hide His action from His servant Abraham, then speaking of the cry from Sodom and Gomorrah and His intended investigation. The narrative supplies a concrete disclosure to a named servant.
source_text: For the Lord God will certainly do no deed unless He reveals His discipline to His servants the prophets.

target_units.text: And the Lord said, “Shall I hide from Abraham My servant what I am doing?
Abraham shall surely become a great and numerous nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him.

For I knew that he would command his sons and his household after him; and they shall keep the ways of the Lord, to do righteousness and judgment, that the Lord may bring upon Abraham all that He has spoken to him.”
And the Lord said, “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has increased, and their sins are exceedingly great.
So I will go down and see whether they are being brought to an end according to their cry which comes to Me; and if not, that I may know.”

relationship: prophetic speech experienced as a compelling burden
rationale: Amos asks who could fail to prophesy after the Lord has spoken. In Jeremiah's account, the resolve not to speak in the Lord's name is overcome by His word becoming like an unbearable fire in the bones. Both portray the difficulty of withholding that speech.
source_text: A lion will roar—and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken—and who will not prophesy?

target_units.text: And I said: I will certainly not name the Lord’s name or speak in His name again. And it became like a burning fire blazing in my bones; I am weakened on every side and cannot bear it.

relationship: same-book identification of oppression on Samaria's mountain
rationale: Amos3 summons outsiders to Samaria's mountain to see the oppression within it. Amos4 addresses the heifers of Bashan on that same mountain and specifies their oppression of the poor and trampling of the needy. The later charge makes the earlier announced oppression more particular.
source_text: Announce to the regions among the Assyrians and to Egypt’s regions: “Gather upon Samaria’s mountain and see the many astonishing things in her midst and the oppression within her!”

target_units.text: Hear this word, heifers of Bashan on Samaria’s mountain, who oppress the poor and trample the needy, who say to their masters, “Give to us so that we may drink!”

relationship: injustice portrayed as something stored
rationale: Amos describes people storing injustice and suffering in their regions. Micah pictures a lawless person's house storing lawless treasures and wealth filled with impiety. The storage imagery connects them, while Micah explicitly names treasures and wealth.
source_text: “She did not know what would be against her,” says the Lord—those storing injustice and suffering in their regions.

target_units.text: Is there not fire, and a lawless person’s house storing lawless treasures, and injustice with insolence?
Will a lawless person be justified with a balance and deceptive weights in a pouch?
From these they filled their wealth with impiety; those inhabiting her spoke falsehoods, and their tongue was exalted in their mouth.

relationship: parallel desolation and plunder addressed to Tyre
rationale: The supplied Amos verse addresses Tyre and announces desolation, lowered strength and plundered regions. Ezekiel's Tyre oracle likewise announces strength brought down, plundered possessions, demolished buildings and a site not rebuilt. The native Tyre address is retained without replacing it with Samaria.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord God: “Tyre, your land will be desolated all around; he will bring down your strength from you, and your regions will be plundered.”

target_units.text: With his horses’ hoofs they will trample all your squares. He will kill your people with the sword and bring the support of your strength down to the ground.
He will plunder your strength, strip your possessions, throw down your walls, and demolish your desirable houses. He will throw your stones, timber, and dust into the sea.
He will put an end to the multitude of your musicians, and the sound of your psalteries will certainly no longer be heard.
I will make you a smooth rock, a drying place for nets. You will certainly not be rebuilt, for I have spoken, says the Lord.

relationship: shepherd rescue from a lion's mouth
rationale: Amos compares the snatching out of Samaria's inhabitants with a shepherd rescuing two legs or an earlobe from a lion. David's account in Samuel likewise describes tending a flock and pulling a sheep from a predator's mouth. Amos's fragmentary rescue remains distinct from David's description.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: “As when a shepherd snatches two legs or an earlobe from a lion’s mouth, so the sons of Israel who dwell in Samaria will be snatched out, opposite a tribe, and priests in Damascus.”

target_units.text: David said to Saul, “Your servant tended his father’s flock. Whenever a lion or a bear came and took a sheep from the herd,
I went after it, struck it, and pulled the sheep from its mouth. If it rose against me, I seized its throat, struck it, and killed it.

relationship: summons to hear a case concerning Israel
rationale: Amos commands hearing and bearing witness to Jacob's house before announcing judgment. Micah likewise summons mountains and hills to hear the Lord's case with Israel. Both frame the indictment with an audience called to hear, without making their audiences identical.
source_text: “Hear and bear witness to Jacob’s house,” says the Lord God Almighty,

target_units.text: Hear now the word of the Lord. The Lord said: “Rise, enter into judgment before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.”
Hear, hills, the Lord’s judgment, and you ravines, foundations of the earth! For the Lord has a case against His people, and He will argue it with Israel.

relationship: judgment involving Bethel's altar
rationale: Amos announces judgment on Bethel's altars and their horns falling to the ground. Kings records a man of God denouncing the altar at Bethel, with a foretold splitting of the altar then occurring as a portent. The shared place and damaged altar connect them; the damage is described differently.
source_text: “because on the day I exact judgment upon Israel for its impieties, I will also exact judgment upon Bethel’s altars. The altar’s horns will be demolished and fall upon the ground,

target_units.text: Behold, a man of God came from Judah to Bethel by the Lord’s word, while Jeroboam stood at the altar to offer sacrifice.

He called to the altar by the Lord’s word: “Altar, altar! Thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to David’s house, Josiah by name. He will sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who offer sacrifice upon you, and he will burn human bones upon you.”
He gave a portent that day, saying, “This is the word the Lord has spoken: Behold, the altar will split, and the fat upon it will pour out.”

When King Jeroboam heard the words of the man of God who had called against the altar in Bethel, the king stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, “Seize him!” Behold, the hand he stretched out against him withered, and he could not draw it back.
The altar split, and the fat poured from the altar, according to the portent the man of God had given by the Lord’s word.

relationship: ivory buildings in Israel's history and announced judgment
rationale: Amos says ivory houses will perish among the houses struck. Kings records the ivory house Ahab built among his royal works. That named building provides a historical example of the distinctive kind of structure named in Amos, without identifying every house in the oracle.
source_text: and I will confound and strike the colonnaded house along with the summer house. Ivory houses will perish, and many other houses will be added,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: The rest of Ahab’s acts, all he did, the ivory house he built, and all the cities he made—behold, are these not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel?

relationship: animal imagery depicting oppression of the vulnerable
rationale: Amos addresses heifers on Samaria's mountain who oppress the poor and trample the needy. Ezekiel depicts strong sheep trampling pasture and forcing out failing sheep, followed by God's judgment between them. Both use animal imagery for the strong harming others under God's scrutiny.
source_text: Hear this word, heifers of Bashan on Samaria’s mountain, who oppress the poor and trample the needy, who say to their masters, “Give to us so that we may drink!”

target_units.text: Was it not enough for you that you grazed the good pasture, yet trampled the rest of your pasture with your feet, drank the settled water and troubled the rest with your feet?
My sheep grazed what your feet had trampled and drank the water troubled by your feet.
Therefore thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I will distinguish between the strong sheep and the weak sheep.
You shove with your sides and shoulders; you butted with your horns and forced out every failing one.
I will save My sheep, and they certainly will no longer be plunder. I will judge between ram and ram.

relationship: divine oath associated with what is holy
rationale: Amos reports the Lord swearing by His holy things before announcing judgment. The psalm reports His oath by His holiness concerning David. Both explicitly associate the Lord's oath with holiness, while the object and purpose are stated differently.
source_text: The Lord swears by His holy things: “Look, days are coming upon you, and they will take you with weapons; fiery pestilences will throw those with you into cauldrons burning underneath,

target_units.text: Once I swore by My holiness: I will not lie to David.

relationship: Gilgal identified with religious wrongdoing
rationale: Amos identifies Gilgal as a place where impiety was multiplied. Hosea likewise locates the people's evils at Gilgal and announces divine rejection because of their wicked practices. The named place and the indictment of its practices closely connect the passages.
source_text: “You entered Bethel and acted lawlessly; at Gilgal you multiplied impiety. You brought your sacrifices for the morning and your tithes for the three-day period,

target_units.text: All their evils are at Gilgal, because there I hated them. Because of their wicked practices I will expel them from My house. I will certainly love them no longer; all their rulers are disobedient.

relationship: shortage of bread within unsuccessful discipline
rationale: Amos announces aching teeth and a shortage of bread, yet says the people did not turn to God. Leviticus likewise warns that failure to accept discipline will bring further punishment, including scarcity of bread and eating without being filled. The shortage and failed corrective response connect them.
source_text: “I will give you aching teeth in all your cities and shortage of bread in all your places; yet you did not turn to Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: And if by these things you are not disciplined, but walk crookedly toward Me,
then I too will walk with you in contrary anger, and I too will strike you seven times in return for your sins.
And I will bring upon you a sword exacting the penalty of the covenant. You shall flee into your cities, and I will send death among you; you shall be handed into enemies’ hands.
When I afflict you with a scarcity of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven and give back your bread by weight. You shall eat and in no wise be filled.

relationship: withheld rainfall as divine judgment
rationale: Amos describes the Lord withholding rain, leaving an unwatered portion dry. Deuteronomy likewise warns that the Lord will shut heaven so there is no rain and the land fails to yield when Israel turns to other gods. Amos's differing treatment of individual cities remains its particular detail.
source_text: “I withheld rainfall from you three months before the vintage. I will rain on one city but not on another; one portion will be watered, and the portion on which I do not rain will dry up,

target_units.text: take heed unto yourself, lest your heart be enlarged, and you transgress, and serve other gods, and bow down unto them,

and the Lord be kindled to wrath against you, and shut up heaven, so that there is no rain, and the land does not yield her fruit, and you perish speedily from the good land which the Lord has given you.

relationship: journeys for water fail during drought
rationale: Amos describes cities assembling at another city to drink without being filled. Jeremiah's drought account similarly sends people to wells only to return with empty vessels because water is absent. Both describe an unsuccessful search for drinking water amid lack of rain.
source_text: and two or three cities will assemble at one city to drink water, yet they certainly will not be filled; and you did not turn to Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: And the Lord’s word came to Jeremiah concerning the lack of rain:
Judea mourned, and her gates were emptied and darkened upon the earth, and Jerusalem’s cry rose.
Her magnates sent their younger ones for water; they came to wells and found no water and brought back their vessels empty.
And the land’s works failed because there was no rain; the farmers were ashamed and covered their heads.

relationship: crop loss followed by failure to turn to the Lord
rationale: Amos describes damaged produce and vineyards, fig orchards and olive groves devoured, followed by the failure to turn to the Lord. Haggai similarly recalls deficient grain and wine yields and struck work, ending with the same failure to turn to Him. Their listed forms of damage remain different.
source_text: “I struck you with burning and jaundice. You multiplied your gardens; the caterpillar devoured your vineyards, fig orchards and olive groves, yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: on how things were with you: when you put twenty sata of barley into a bin, there were ten sata of barley; when you went to the wine vat to draw fifty metretai, there were twenty.
I struck you with barrenness, damage from wind and hail—all the works of your hands—and you did not turn to Me, says the Lord.

relationship: death and sword within divine punishment
rationale: Amos announces death, young men killed by the sword and captivity involving horses. Leviticus likewise announces a covenant-penalty sword, death among the people and their being handed to enemies. The combined death, sword and enemy defeat connect the warnings without importing Amos's Egypt-road detail into Leviticus.
source_text: “I sent death among you on Egypt’s road and killed your young men with the sword, along with the captivity of your horses. I brought your camps up in fire in My anger; yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: And I will bring upon you a sword exacting the penalty of the covenant. You shall flee into your cities, and I will send death among you; you shall be handed into enemies’ hands.

relationship: explicit recollection of Sodom and Gomorrah's overthrow
rationale: Amos expressly compares the people's overthrow with God's overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. Genesis narrates fire upon those cities, their overthrow and Lot sent out from its midst, supplying the named event recalled by the comparison.
source_text: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a firebrand snatched from fire. Yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.
And his wife looked behind her, and became a pillar of salt.
And Abraham rose early in the morning, and went to the place where he had stood before the Lord.
And he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward the land of the surrounding country; and he saw, and behold, a flame rose from the earth as the vapour of a furnace.
And when the Lord blotted out all the cities of the surrounding country, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out from the midst of the overthrow, when the Lord overthrew the cities where Lot lived.

relationship: shared image of a firebrand pulled from fire
rationale: Amos describes the people as a firebrand snatched from fire after their overthrow. Zechariah presents Joshua before the Lord's angel and compares him with a brand pulled from fire. The shared rescue image is explicit, with different persons and settings.
source_text: “I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a firebrand snatched from fire. Yet not even so did you turn to Me,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, with the slanderer standing at his right hand to oppose him.
The Lord said to the slanderer, “May the Lord rebuke you, slanderer! May the Lord, who chose Jerusalem, rebuke you! Look, is this not like a brand pulled from fire?”

relationship: call upon God in the setting of return
rationale: Amos commands Israel to prepare to call upon God after repeatedly saying they had not turned to Him. Isaiah likewise commands seeking and calling upon God and the ungodly person's return to the Lord for mercy. Amos's native call-upon wording is preserved.
source_text: “Therefore this is what I will do to you, Israel. Since I will do this to you, prepare to call upon your God, Israel!”

target_units.text: Seek God, and when you find Him, call upon Him; and when He draws near to you,
let the ungodly forsake his ways, and the lawless man his counsels; and let him return to the Lord, and he will receive mercy; for He will abundantly forgive your sins.

relationship: the Lord's control of wind and weather
rationale: Amos identifies the Lord as establishing thunder and creating wind, alongside His other acts. The psalm likewise describes the Lord's deeds across heaven, earth and seas, including lightning for rain and winds brought from His treasuries. Both attribute these weather phenomena to His power.
source_text: For look, I am the One establishing thunder and creating wind, announcing His anointed to human beings, making dawn and mist, and stepping upon the earth’s heights. The Lord God Almighty is His name.

target_units.text: Everything the Lord willed, He did, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all the deeps.
He brings clouds up from the earth’s extremity; He made lightning for rain; He brings winds out of His treasuries.
